Eurovision party — the complete hosting playbook

A Eurovision party is a watch party for the Eurovision Song Contest, usually styled as a costume night with themed food, voting games, and rowdy commentary. Done right, it is the most chaotic dinner party of the year. Here is how to run one — guest list, theme, food, run-of-show, and how to keep every song competitive.

What is a Eurovision party?

A Eurovision party is a structured watch night built around the grand final of the Eurovision Song Contest. The broadcast lasts roughly three and a half hours; a good party turns that runtime into a competition by adding three ingredients: opinions (everyone has a take), stakes (a scored game makes every song matter), and sustained energy (food, costumes, and breaks structured around the broadcast). Skip any one and you get a quiet living-room screening — fun, but not a party.

Headcount and venue

  • 2–20 players via the app. Sweet spot is 6–10 — enough variety in predictions and duels without the trivia rotation getting stale.
  • Living room, garden, or Zoom. The scoring app runs on every guest's phone, so the venue just has to fit the broadcast and the buffet.
  • Broadcast source. National broadcaster (BBC, RAI, ARD, ERT, etc.), the official Eurovision YouTube stream where available, or a projector pulled from any of the above.
  • One screen for the show, one for the leaderboard. A second screen mirroring the live Dashboard keeps the standings visible without anyone craning at a phone.

Theme and decor

  • National flag bunting. Print the 26 grand-final flags and string them across the room — cheapest, most legible decor on the night.
  • A mini disco ball. One on a battery base in the buffet area is enough to tilt the whole room into Eurovision territory.
  • Battery-powered LED lights. Pink and purple to match the broadcast palette; tape them along the screen frame.
  • Country assignments. Each guest draws a country at the door from a bowl and roots for it all night — instant emotional investment.

Food and drink — country-themed buffet

Pick six countries from the running order and serve one dish per country, all finger food (no plating during the show). A representative spread:

  • Sweden — meatballs with lingonberry.
  • Italy — arancini and bruschetta.
  • Greece — spanakopita triangles.
  • UK — sausage rolls.
  • France — mini croissants with brie.
  • Israel — hummus with pita.

Drinks: country-themed cocktails (Aperol for Italy, Aquavit for Sweden, Ouzo for Greece, Pastis for France) plus a generous mocktail option for designated drivers and non-drinkers.

Run-of-show — 4-hour timeline

Times are relative to broadcast start (T-0 = first song). Anchor everything around T-0 and the night runs itself.

TimeWhat happensWhat to do
T-60Doors openCountry draw, costume judging, first drink
T-45Open the roomShare the join code; tap Start the Party! once everyone is in — predictions, quiz and duels open
T-30Picks and warm-upEveryone fills in Top 5 / Worst 5 and plays quiz round 1; final buffet top-up
T-0Broadcast startsPredictions stay editable through the songs; quiz and duels keep running
T+0–2:0026 entries airDuels run during postcards and ad breaks
T+2:00Interval act (~25 min)Big duel window; hot food drop
T+2:30Voting opensLines open for jury + televote; the app locks predictions, quiz and duels automatically
T+3:00Jury voteMost chaotic 25 minutes on TV
T+3:30Televote + winnerOfficial results land in the room automatically
T+3:45Trophy revealFive winners in the app; photos

Game options to layer on

Eurovision Games stacks four scoring modes across the night — pick all four for full chaos, or just predictions if you want a quieter room.

  • Predictions — Top 5 and Worst 5, editable until voting opens. The 500-point spine of the leaderboard.
  • Quiz — three rounds each player plays at their own pace, before and during the show, until voting opens.
  • Duels — head-to-head trivia in the ad breaks. Steal or Double.
  • Dashboard — the live leaderboard everyone in the room is watching.

Hosting in different time zones

Eurovision broadcasts live in CEST, which is mid-evening for most of Europe and an hour earlier in the UK, Ireland, and Portugal. In the Americas it is midday to mid-afternoon; in Australia and New Zealand it lands early on Sunday morning. Match the food to the local slot — breakfast spreads in Sydney, full dinner in Berlin — but keep the run-of-show identical: doors at T-60, predictions locked when voting opens, duels in the breaks. The room link works the same in every time zone.
